name: Ministry of Science Research & Technology
description: Iran’s Ministry of Science, Research and Technology is a central institution in the governance of general higher education. Its responsibilities must be distinguished from those of the Ministry of Health and Medical Education, which oversees medical universities and related education.

seo.title: Iran’s Ministry of Science, Research and Technology | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s general higher-education ministry, its relationship with medical education, university funding, and the limits of available evidence.

content.heading: A ministry within a divided education system
content.content:
Iran’s Ministry of Science, Research and Technology, commonly abbreviated MSRT, belongs to a higher-education system whose responsibilities are divided among institutions. UNESCO’s education profile places basic sciences, humanities, engineering, arts and agriculture within its sphere, while medical universities and clinical education fall under the Ministry of Health and Medical Education. The distinction matters when interpreting a university’s affiliation or an announcement described simply as an Iranian higher-education policy. [s1]

School education has a different institutional home: UNESCO identifies the Ministry of Education as responsible for state and non-state education from pre-primary through secondary levels. Consequently, MSRT should not be treated as a single ministry directing every stage and subject of Iranian education. An institution’s educational level, subject area and affiliation all matter. [s1]

content.heading: University funding and student support
content.content:
UNESCO’s financing profile describes MSRT as allocating and overseeing funds for general universities, alongside a separate medical-university financing channel through the health ministry. It also describes government scholarships administered through MSRT, distinguishing support covering tuition and a stipend from support covering tuition alone. These descriptions establish funding arrangements; they do not establish that every institution or applicant receives equivalent support. [s2]

The same profile describes higher education as partly subsidized rather than universally tuition-free. For international readers, this is a useful correction to the assumption that public responsibility automatically means education without charges. Institution-specific fees and scholarship eligibility require separate verification. [s2]

content.heading: University governance and freedom of expression
content.content:
Administrative responsibilities do not by themselves establish the conditions in which students study or researchers work. Human Rights Watch’s World Report 2025 documented university disciplinary measures against students for peaceful expression during its reporting period. That evidence concerns university governance in practice and should be read alongside institutional accounts of education administration. It does not establish that MSRT personally directed every documented disciplinary decision. [s3]

A careful assessment therefore needs both institutional evidence and evidence from affected students and staff. Funding, academic provision and freedom of expression are distinct questions; progress or formal commitments in one area cannot be used as proof of outcomes in another.

content.heading: What remains to be established
content.content: This account establishes the ministry’s place within a divided education system, but it is not a complete description of its legal powers. A publication-ready institutional profile still requires an inspected mandate, a current organizational chart and documentation explaining the ministry’s relationships with research institutes and technology organizations. The ministry’s English website could not be retrieved during this research. No current officeholder, contact details or organizational performance claim is therefore presented.

name: Plan & Budget Organization
description: Iran’s Plan and Budget Organization connects development planning with preparation of the national budget. Its coordinating role is distinct from parliamentary approval, treasury functions and the delivery of services by spending agencies.

seo.title: Iran’s Plan and Budget Organization | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore the distinction between Iran’s development planning, budget preparation, parliamentary approval and expenditure implementation.

content.heading: Connecting priorities with public spending
content.content:
The Plan and Budget Organization, abbreviated PBO, occupies the junction between development priorities and annual spending decisions. UNESCO’s higher-education financing profile identifies it as the organization preparing the national budget, which Parliament approves. University funding provides a concrete example of why this coordinating role matters: sector institutions depend on decisions made within a wider allocation process. [s1]

Preparing a budget is analytically different from approving it, releasing funds or delivering a service. Keeping those stages separate helps readers assess whether a government announcement describes a proposal, legal authorization or expenditure that actually occurred.

content.heading: The documented planning framework
content.content:
A World Bank assessment published in November 2005 describes the Management and Planning Organization, or MPO, as preparing development plans in consultation with sector ministries and universities. Its budget-process table separates preparation by the planning organization from Cabinet approval, parliamentary appropriation and implementation by executive bodies. This is historical evidence about the planning machinery, rather than confirmation that every procedure remains unchanged. [s2]

The report traces the first substantial plan and planning organization to 1949. It also describes agency performance reporting as part of the relationship between development plans and budget requests. The important institutional distinction is between setting a coordinated framework and carrying out individual programs. A central planning body can review proposals without itself operating each school, hospital or infrastructure project. [s2]

content.heading: Planning, treasury and audit
content.content:
Encyclopaedia Iranica’s historical account distinguishes PBO’s work on plans and budgets from revenue collection and treasury functions undertaken by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Finance. It also describes parliamentary audit as a separate stage. These distinctions help explain why a single budget document involves several institutions with different responsibilities. [s3]

That account discusses PBO oversight of development budgets and project completion. Such responsibilities should not be read as evidence that all projects were completed or that spending achieved its intended benefits. Monitoring arrangements describe how performance is supposed to be examined; an assessment of results requires expenditure records, implementation reports and independent scrutiny. [s3]

content.heading: Reading budget claims carefully
content.content:
The inspected evidence supports an introductory account of budget coordination, but not a current procedural manual. In particular, the historical World Bank report uses the MPO name, while UNESCO’s more recent profile uses PBO. Those documents alone do not establish a complete chronology of reorganizations. [s1][s2]

For a particular spending claim, the next research step is to identify the relevant budget year and distinguish the proposed amount, enacted allocation and reported expenditure. Until those records are inspected, neither a development target nor a budget announcement establishes completed implementation.

name: Judicial & Legal Institutions
description: Iran’s judicial and legal institutions include courts, administrative review bodies and the legal profession. Understanding them requires distinguishing constitutional responsibilities, the jurisdiction of particular bodies and documented conditions of access to justice.

seo.title: Judicial and Legal Institutions in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An introduction to Iran’s courts, judicial administration, administrative review and legal profession, distinguishing constitutional rules from documented practice.

content.heading: Judicial authority and administration
content.content:
Iran’s Constitution describes the judiciary as an independent power, while providing for the Supreme Leader to appoint its head. Article 158 assigns that head responsibility for judicial organization, judicial bills and the administration of judges. Constitutional independence is therefore a formal description that must be examined alongside appointment arrangements and documented practice. [s1]

The Minister of Justice has a different constitutional function: managing relations between the judiciary and the executive and legislative branches. The minister should not be confused with the head of the judiciary. [s1]

content.heading: Different courts answer different questions
content.content:
The GlobaLex legal-system guide distinguishes general courts from courts with specific jurisdiction. Its account explains that general jurisdiction is subject to exceptions established for particular courts. It also distinguishes civil and criminal proceedings and describes appellate review. This is a useful starting point for understanding why the nature of a dispute matters before identifying the appropriate institution. [s2]

An appeal should not be assumed to follow one identical route in every case. The guide separately discusses criminal courts, the Supreme Court and administrative adjudication. Readers need to establish the type of proceeding and the applicable legislation before interpreting a reference to review by a higher court. The guide was published in 2022 and cannot by itself establish later procedural changes. [s2]

content.title: Selected constitutional relationships
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  L["Supreme Leader"] -->|"Appoints under Article 157"| H["Head of the judiciary"]
  H -->|"Organizes under Article 158"| J["Judicial administration"]
  S["Supreme Court"] -->|"Supervises application of law under Article 161"| C["Courts"]
  A["Administrative Justice Court"] -->|"Reviews complaints under Article 173"| G["Government officials and units"]
```
content.summary: The arrows identify selected legal functions. They do not represent every institution or every route of appeal.

content.heading: Review, reasons and legal representation
content.content:
The Constitution gives the Supreme Court a role in supervising lawful adjudication and ensuring uniform judicial practice. It separately provides for the Administrative Justice Court to examine complaints against governmental officials, units and regulations. Administrative review is thus a distinct constitutional function. [s1]

Constitutional safeguards also include reasoned judgments, protection against compelled confessions and a right to legal representation. These provisions establish standards against which proceedings can be assessed; their presence does not establish compliance in an individual case. [s1]

content.heading: Formal safeguards and documented violations
content.content:
Human Rights Watch’s World Report 2025 describes systemic due-process and fair-trial violations in the repression of anti-government protests. It reports that Revolutionary Court judges failed to address allegations of torture and ill-treatment, including in proceedings resulting in death sentences. These findings concern documented practice and qualify any account based solely on constitutional guarantees. [s3]

At a March 2025 press conference, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran reported serious fair-trial and due-process violations in the repression of the protests that began in 2022. Its findings included violations affecting children and persecution of lawyers and others acting in solidarity with victims. These are findings of an investigative mission, rather than criminal judgments determining the liability of every implicated individual. [s4]

The distinction between institutional design and implementation is essential. A diagram can explain a legal responsibility; it cannot demonstrate that a defendant received independent representation, that evidence was lawfully obtained or that a remedy was effective.

content.heading: How to explore this subject
content.content:
The pages in this branch separate general courts, appellate courts, the Supreme Court and administrative justice. They also provide distinct entries for property-registration institutions and bar associations. This organization helps keep adjudication, administrative services and professional representation conceptually separate.

For any specific legal question, a reliable account needs the relevant legislation, its amendment history and evidence about implementation. This overview does not establish filing requirements, deadlines or available remedies in an individual dispute. Its central purpose is to identify institutional distinctions and the evidence needed to evaluate them.
